setup.zh: 十月十三。你断着一根肋骨，怀里揣着舅舅的信：「你爹如今天天进黑松岭……膝盖比去年重了。」柴房里，饭桶。
setup.en: The thirteenth of the tenth month. A rib is broken, and in your coat is your uncle's letter: "Your father goes into the Heisong Ridge every day now… his knee is worse than last year." In the woodshed: Rice Bucket.

recap.zh: 开饭桶：两块灵石开出一颗含笑半步颠，银月一根尾巴毛开出一张踏马的符，一肚子灵气喂到见底，开出一颗九道金纹的回春丹。你没吃，装进辣椒油瓶，留给爹的膝盖；断着一根肋骨巡了半个月的夜。月底盘账，褚先生按出那根骨头：「这根骨头，还断着。」
recap.en: Feeding Rice Bucket: two spirit stones brought out a Smiling Half-Step Topple, one of Silver Moon's hairs a stamping talisman, and a bellyful of qi poured to the last drop one spring-return pill with nine gold lines. You didn't eat it; you put it in a chilli-oil bottle, kept for your father's knee, and walked the night watch half a month on a broken rib. At the month-end reckoning Master Chu found the bone: "This bone is still broken."

zh: 两块灵石喂进去，「咯嘣、咯嘣」。
en: A bellyful of qi, pushed to the last drop.

story.zh:
门外「笃笃笃」三声。他手忙脚乱，一把将小狰捞过来，往炉子上一放。小狰正睡得迷糊，四只爪子一抱，把炉子搂在肚皮底下，五条尾巴往上一盖，只露出一个红毛团子。小满把门拉得大开，自己往门框上一靠，身子把屋里挡了一半。

是周衡。他抱着账簿，看了看小满肿得只剩一条缝的左眼，看了看他捂着肋骨的那只手，道：「马师弟一早来过执事房。说你摔坏了，起不来，药园这几夜，他替你巡。」他顿了一顿，「我去园门口看了巡夜簿。昨夜那一格，有一个手印。」他没说那手印是什么颜色。小满道：「是我按的。今夜，我也巡。」周衡道：「你这个样子。」小满道：「巡得了。」周衡低头提笔，在账簿上写了一行，吹了吹墨：「月底盘账，只认账，不认脸。」说罢，抱着账簿走了。

小满想了很久，才想明白：昨天夜里的事，周衡知道；周衡也只认他那本账。

他把门闩上，从小狰肚皮底下把饭桶抠了出来。银月那几句没说完的话，他在心里排了一夜：喂它，它吐东西。他把怀里剩下的两块灵石塞进它肚里，两只手按在铜肚子上。盖子底下「咯嘣、咯嘣」两声，像人嚼炒豆，嚼得很香。跟着他手心一凉：丹田里那股暖，像水进了沙子，给它吸了过去。吸到第七口，「咔哒」一声，盖子跳开了。

一股香气冲了出来。肚里躺着一颗丹，桂圆大小，粉里透红，丹身上一道红纹，两头往上翘，像一张抿着嘴的笑脸。那香气比马小宝的桂花糕香十倍，香得小狰直立起来，口水挂了一尺长。小满捧着它，香得自己也咧开了嘴，往窗口亮处走——只迈了半步，绊着小狰，一个跟头栽进柴堆里，脸上还笑着。

胸口的木牌温了一温，一个尖鼻子从衣领里探出来，抽了两抽。银月的声音困得发黏：「……什么味儿？」她闻了又闻：「闻着是好东西。好东西，不见得是给人吃的。」小满道：「那它叫什么？」银月瞧了瞧他，又瞧了瞧小狰：「你捧着它，笑了，走了半步，栽了。」打了个哈欠，「……含笑半步颠。」小满没敢吃，拿油纸包了三层，塞进腰带里头的夹层——娘缝来装铜钱的，一回也没装过钱。

银月的爪子却没缩回去：「看好了。本王给你开个张。」她从尾巴尖上拔下一根银毛，疼得龇了一龇牙，丢进饭桶。盖上那只小兽睁开一只眼睛，瞧了瞧她，把身子扭了过去，拿屁股对着她。「咔哒」，里头飘出一张黄纸来，落在他膝盖上。朱砂画的一匹马：脑袋大，身子小，四条腿画得一般长，像四根筷子插在一个馒头上；四只蹄子底下各点了一个圈，倒像这马正抬着蹄子往下踏；尾巴画成一道弯钩，一直勾到纸边上。小满翻过来，背面什么也没有。他憋了半天，憋出一句：「……这踏马的，是什么符？」

银月盯着那匹马瞧了一会儿，脸上的毛都嫌弃得竖了起来：「本王的一根毛。就换这个。」又瞧了一眼，「画成这个样子。还不如本王给你画。」爪子一缩，又睡过去了。木牌凉了一凉，那条尾巴，又暗下去一截。小满这才明白：它不吃白饭，摸它一下，便要吃人一口。

那道踏马的符，他翻过来、掉过去看了半天，不知道该贴在哪儿，也不知道是做什么用的。银月刚嫌过它画成这个样子，他也当它是一张废纸；可那是她拔了一根尾巴毛换来的，扔了，又舍不得。他把它叠成一个小方块，跟那颗含笑半步颠一起，塞进了腰带夹层。他在本子上记了一行：**踏马的符。不知何用。**

他靠着柴墩坐下来。他想要的，只是一样接得上骨头的东西。灵石没了，只剩丹田里那点暖。他两只手按上铜肚子，把那点暖一口一口推了进去，推到见底，还在推。饭桶「咕嘟咕嘟」吸得像一头喝水的牛；井见了底，他眼前一黑，额头磕在盖子上。

「咔哒」。

肚里躺着一颗丹，碧绿碧绿，透亮得像一滴凝住了的露水，一股青苦的回春藤味儿。丹身上有纹，他数了一遍，又数了一遍：九道，全是金的，一道挨着一道，像一个人一圈一圈地系着腰带。一肚子灵气，一颗丹。

他知道一道纹是什么样子：舅舅说过，济世堂柜台上的琉璃罐子里也摆着回春丹，灰扑扑的，一道纹，几个黑点，一颗要五两银子。他手里这一颗，九道。
story.en:
*Tock tock tock* at the door. In a flurry he grabbed Little Zheng and plonked it on the furnace. Little Zheng, half asleep, hugged the furnace under its belly with all four paws and laid its five tails over the top, so only a red ball of fur showed. Xiaoman pulled the door wide open, leaned on the frame, and blocked half the room with his body.

It was Zhou Heng. Holding his ledger, he looked at Xiaoman's left eye swollen to a slit, at the hand holding his ribs. "Brother Ma came to the stewards' office first thing. Says you had a bad fall and can't get up, and he'll watch the herb garden for you these next few nights." He paused. "I went and looked at the watch book by the garden gate. Last night's box has a handprint in it." He didn't say what colour the handprint was. Xiaoman said, "I made it. Tonight I'll watch too." Zhou Heng said, "In this state." Xiaoman said, "I can watch." Zhou Heng lowered his head, wrote a line in the ledger and blew on the ink. "Month-end accounts: I go by the books, not by faces." And he went off with the ledger.

It took Xiaoman a long time to understand: Zhou Heng knew what had happened last night; and Zhou Heng went only by his books.

He barred the door and dug Rice Bucket out from under Little Zheng's belly. All night he had been laying out Silver Moon's unfinished words: feed it, and it spits something out. He pushed his last two spirit stones into its belly and pressed both hands on the bronze. Under the lid came two crunches, *crack, crack*, like someone chewing roasted beans, and enjoying them. Then his palms went cold: the warmth in his belly went into it like water into sand. At the seventh draw there was a *click*, and the lid sprang open.

A fragrance burst out. In its belly lay a pill the size of a longan, pink shading to red, with one red line round it that turned up at both ends, like a mouth pressed shut on a smile. It smelled ten times sweeter than Ma Xiaobao's osmanthus cakes — Little Zheng sat bolt upright with a foot of drool hanging. Xiaoman held it, the smell making him grin too, and walked toward the light at the window — took half a step, tripped over Little Zheng, went head over heels into the woodpile, still smiling.

The token on his chest warmed, and a pointed nose came out at his collar and twitched twice. Silver Moon's voice was sticky with sleep: "…What's that smell?" She sniffed and sniffed. "Smells like something good. Good things aren't always meant for eating." Xiaoman said, "Then what's it called?" Silver Moon looked at him, then at Little Zheng. "You held it, you smiled, you took half a step, you went down." She yawned. "…Smiling Half-Step Topple." Xiaoman didn't dare eat it; he wrapped it in three layers of oiled paper and tucked it into the pocket inside his belt — his mother had sewn it for coppers, and it had never once held a copper.

But Silver Moon's paw didn't go back in. "Watch. I'll open the shop for you." She plucked a single silver hair from the tip of her tail, baring her teeth at the sting, and dropped it into Rice Bucket. The little beast on the lid opened one eye, looked at her, and turned round to show her its backside. *Click* — out floated a sheet of yellow paper and landed on his knee. A horse in cinnabar: big head, small body, four legs drawn all the same length like four chopsticks stuck in a steamed bun; under each hoof a little circle, as if the horse were lifting its feet to stamp; the tail a single hook curling right to the edge of the paper. Xiaoman turned it over: nothing on the back. He held it in a long while, and what came out was: "…What the stamping hell kind of talisman is this?"

Silver Moon stared at the horse for a while, the fur on her face standing up in disgust. "One of my hairs. For this." Another look. "Drawn like that. I could draw you a better one myself." The paw went in, and she was asleep again. The token cooled a little, and that one tail dimmed a notch further. Only then did Xiaoman understand: it never eats for free; touch it once, and it takes a bite of you.

The stamping talisman he turned this way and that for a long while: he had no idea where it was meant to stick, or what it was for. Silver Moon had just sneered at the drawing, and he took it for scrap too; but she had paid a hair from her tail for it, and he couldn't bring himself to throw it away. He folded it into a small square and tucked it into the pocket inside his belt, alongside the Smiling Half-Step Topple. He wrote one line in his book: **Stamping talisman. Use unknown.**

He sat down against the chopping block. All he wanted was one thing that could knit a bone. The stones were gone; only the warmth in his belly was left. He pressed both hands to the bronze and pushed that warmth in, mouthful by mouthful, pushed it to the bottom and kept pushing. Rice Bucket drank with a *glug, glug*, like an ox at a trough; the well ran dry, his sight went black, and his forehead hit the lid.

*Click.*

In its belly lay one pill, jade green, clear as a drop of frozen dew, with the bitter green smell of spring-return vine. There were lines on it; he counted them once, and again: nine, all gold, one next to another round the pill, like a man winding a sash round his waist turn by turn. A bellyful of qi, one pill.

He knew what one line looked like: his uncle had said the Jishi Hall kept spring-return pills in a glass jar on the counter, dull grey, one line, a few black spots, five taels apiece. The one in his hand had nine.

exits.means: keeps the pill in a chilli-oil bottle for his father's knee, and keeps the night watch half a month on a broken rib

story.zh:
他把丹托在手心里，肋骨一抽一抽地疼。他知道这东西能做什么：吞下去，今夜断的骨头便接上了，肿便消了，今夜、明夜、往后的每一夜，他都能好好地站在药园里，月底稳稳地过账。马小宝那半句话，就落空了。

他把丹送到嘴边。

怀里那封信硌了他一下。**膝盖比去年重了，阴天下不了炕，晴天照去。**他爹拖着那条腿，一个人过断碑，往黑松岭里走，为的是两只兔子。

炉盖上那只小兽睁着眼睛，看着他。

他把手放了下来。

伙房的胖大娘有一只装辣椒油的小瓷瓶，空了要扔，他去伙房讨了来，在井边洗了七遍，还是一股辣味儿。他把那颗丹装了进去，塞紧，揣进怀里，贴着那封信。他在本子上只记了一行：**九纹回春丹一颗，在瓶里。给爹的膝盖。**

捎是捎不下去的。一个进门一个月、交不起公中的杂灵根，捎回家一颗济世堂一辈子没见过的丹，马三在门框上敲着短棍问：沈老大，你儿子在山上，偷了谁家的？他借了药房的笔，给舅舅回了一行：儿好，勿念。叫爹别进黑松岭。又摸出三文钱——他身上统共只有这三文——塞给那光脚的孩子。那孩子捏着三文钱，看了他半天，道：「你舅舅说了，三文钱他给过了。」把钱又塞了回来，挑起担子走了。

那天夜里，子时，他翻不过墙，照旧从豁口里爬出去，爬到药园，在巡夜簿上十三夜那一格，按了一个手印。

那以后的半个月，沈小满是断着一根肋骨巡的夜。

白天，他照旧去讲堂，照旧挑水，挑一担，歇三回，肩膀不敢换。饭堂里，马小宝天天端着空碗从他桌边经过，天天停一停，拿指头戳那一个地方：「师弟，好些了没有？」戳一下，他眼前白一下，嘴上道：「好些了，师兄。」

夜里，他坐在药园东角阿禾那一圈红线旁边，灵草中间。肋骨疼，一口气吸不到底，他就不吸到底，学那个萝卜筐里的孩子，肚子一鼓，一落，浅浅的，落得长长的。灵草夜里吐出来的那点气，稠得像娘过年熬的那一锅粥，一口一口落下去，肚子底下那一团暖，一夜往下坠一丝。小狰蹲在他脚边，冲着黑地里，一声不吭。

十五夜里，墙头上「沙」的一响，冒出一个脑袋来。小满没动。那人骑在墙头上，四下里张望，张望到他这里，停住了。

是老蔫。

月亮底下，两个人隔着半个园子，看了很久。一个坐在灵草中间，脸上还青着；一个骑在墙头上，手里攥着一只空布袋。老蔫的嘴动了动，什么也没说出来。他慢慢地，从墙头上退了回去，脚下一滑，墙外「咕咚」一声，接着是一瘸一拐、走远了的脚步。

天亮以后，小满在墙根草里捡到一张油纸，叠成方块，还带着一点甜香，纸角上印着一个红戳——县城那家点心铺子的戳。整个沉鼎观，吃得起这家桂花糕的，只有一个人。他把油纸夹进了巡夜簿里。巡夜簿上那一夜，他写：**墙头有人，回去了。没丢。紫玉参，四十一。**

十月廿二，天刚亮，柴房的门给人一脚踹开了。马小宝站在门口，身后是周衡，再后头是他的跟班，手上缠白布的那一个也在。马小宝一把掀开小狰睡觉的那堆干草——草底下，赫然躺着一株紫玉参，叶子还是鲜的。「药园最值钱的东西。」马小宝道，「畜生就是畜生，改不了偷。巡夜的养贼，周师兄，您怎么记？」

小满蹲下去，把那株参拈起来，看它的茬口。十月初九药园西头那株给啃了的灵草，茬口是齐的，却是毛的，一口咬断，牙印一道一道。这一株的茬口，是光的，斜斜的一道，平得像镜子。「师兄，」他把参递给周衡，「狰是拿牙啃的。这一株，是拿刀切的。药园的紫玉参，一共四十一株，我夜夜数一遍，巡夜簿上都记着数。今早卯时我从园子里出来，还是四十一株。这一株，不是药园的。」

周衡起身便往药园走。一炷香以后回来，账簿上添了一行：**十月廿二，紫玉参，四十一，一株不少。**小狰从小满脚边钻出来，冲着门口那个手缠白布的跟班，抽了两抽鼻子，「咔」地叫了一声。那跟班把手往身后一藏。周衡道：「这一株，账上不记。」抱着账簿走了。马小宝弯腰捡起那株参，捏了一捏，一脚踩烂了。

月底，还有六天。

到了十月廿五那一夜，他坐在灵草中间，一口气落下去，肚子底下「咚」的一声，那一团暖猛地往下一沉，沉得更深，像一块干了一冬的地，一镢头刨下去，又刨出一层来；刨开了，能盛的，一下子多了一倍。练气二层。

是他一夜一夜，断着一根肋骨，自己坐出来的。

十月廿八，周衡盘月底的账，盘到药园那一页，天已擦黑。小满在执事房门口候着；马小宝也在，身后跟着手缠白布的那个，还有老蔫，站在门槛外头。周衡拿指头点着账簿念：「初十，入账灵兽一只。初十至今日，药园丢——」他抬眼看了看门框上那一位，又低下头，「零。」

小满把巡夜簿里夹着的那张油纸抽出来，放在账簿上：「十五夜里，墙头上来过一个人，看了一眼，回去了。墙根底下，掉了这个。」纸角一个红戳。门槛外头，老蔫的脸一下子白了。小满没有看他。

马小宝把桂花糕从嘴里拿了出来：「一张油纸，谁知道是哪儿捡的？」他一步跨进门来，指着小满，「零？那是他自己吃了！周师兄，一个漏勺，进门一个月，夜夜坐在灵草堆里，草叶子都往他身上歪——偷了灵草吃，吃出一层来！」

小满道：「师兄怎么知道，我夜夜坐在灵草堆里？」

执事房里静了下来。马小宝张着嘴，看看周衡，看看房梁，半天才缓过一口气来，声音反倒高了：「……你请人验！请褚先生来，看他是一层，还是二层！」

这一句，是真刀子。一个漏勺，一个月二层——这话要是传开了，不用马小宝再说一个字，全外门都会替他往下想。

小满没去看马小宝。他对周衡道：「师兄，请褚先生来验。」

褚先生是给人从讲堂里请过来的，山羊胡子一翘一翘，很不耐烦。他也不多话，一把扣住小满的手腕。一股凉丝丝的气，从他腕子上钻了进来，顺着经脉，一路往里探。小满闭上眼睛。这是那个萝卜筐里的孩子教他的——一鼓，一落，不拽，不赶。他把那一团二层的暖，一点一点地往下收，收成一粒，收进肚子底下最深的那个地方，拿一口气压住，像把一块烧红的炭，攥进手心里，还不许手松开。褚先生那股气探进来，碰到哪里，哪里便像给铁刷子刷了一下。他咬着牙，照着那个不深不浅的口子喘，一口气碰着肋骨，疼得眼前发白，还得压着。鼻子底下一热，一道血淌了下来，淌到嘴唇上，是咸的。

褚先生探了足有一盏茶的工夫，才松了手，哼了一声：「练气一层，气又薄又散，一碰就流鼻血。漏勺还是漏勺。」他又按了按小满的肋骨，按到左边那一根，手停住了。小满没出声，额头上的汗一颗一颗往下掉。

「这根骨头，还断着。」褚先生道，「半个月了。」他转过身，冲马小宝道，「药园的灵草，治伤最灵。他要是偷吃了一株，这根骨头早长上了。」

马小宝一口桂花糕正咽到一半，呛在了喉咙里，咳得弯下腰去，也没咳出一句话来。

褚先生走到门口，又停住，回过头来，多看了小满一眼，看他鼻子底下那道血，看他捂着肋骨的那只手，到底什么也没问，走了。

周衡把巡夜簿合上，压在账簿底下，道：「只认账，不认脸。」提起笔来写道：**药园巡夜：沈小满。工钱：残株，月一篮。**从桌子底下拎出一只竹篮来，篮里是这个月拔下来的残株：虫咬的，长歪的，灵气散了一半的，堆了小半篮。

小满拎着篮子走出执事房，那一粒被他攥了一盏茶工夫的暖，这时候才敢松开，一松开，便在他身子里翻了三个滚，翻得他扶着墙，咳出一口血来。他擦了擦嘴。怀里那只辣椒油瓶，隔着衣裳，硌着那根没长好的骨头。

他把篮子搁在地上，掏出本子，翻到「兔，十一，九」那一行底下，一笔一画地写：**十月十二。柴房。廿三下。马小宝。**

写完，他在底下画了一道杠，杠底下空着一格。那一格，留着写还的那一天。

那天夜里，外门后院的井台边上，马小宝一个人蹲着，拿井水洗下巴。他拿皂角搓，拿井台上的粗砂磨，磨得下巴通红，那三个黑点还在。他从怀里摸出装聚气丹的瓷瓶，倒过来，往手心里磕。磕出来三颗，是这个月剩下的最后三颗，灰扑扑的，一道纹，纹边上一圈黑点，跟他下巴上的一模一样。

他想起沈小满那根断着的骨头，想起周衡账簿上那张油纸，想起那一颗筑基丹——腊月，冠军，全观就这一颗。他想：他凭什么？他又想：他吃一口，我吃三口。

他把那三颗丹，一口吞了下去，连水都没喝，干咽，咽得脖子一伸一伸的。那股暖升上来了，热烘烘的，烧得他满脸通红，烧得下巴上那三个黑点一跳一跳地疼。他咬着牙，指甲抠进井台的石缝里，等它过去。他站起身来，擦了擦嘴，从袖子里又摸出一块桂花糕，咬了一口。还是饿。

第二天一早，外门的告示栏上，贴出了一张新的告示，墨迹还没干：

**沉鼎秘境，十年一开。冬月初一，外门弟子皆可入。**
story.en:
He held the pill in his palm, his ribs throbbing. He knew what it could do: swallow it, and tonight the broken bone would knit and the swelling go down; tonight, tomorrow night, every night after, he could stand properly in the herb garden and pass the month-end accounts without a wobble. Ma Xiaobao's half-sentence would come to nothing.

He lifted the pill to his mouth.

The letter in his coat dug into him. **His knee is worse than last year — on overcast days he can't get off the kang, and on clear days he goes anyway.** His father dragging that leg past the broken stele alone, into the Heisong Ridge, for the sake of two rabbits.

The little beast on the lid had its eyes open, watching him.

He lowered his hand.

The fat auntie in the kitchen had a little porcelain chilli-oil bottle, empty and about to be thrown out; he went to the kitchen and begged it, and washed it seven times at the well, and it still smelled of chilli. He put the pill in, stoppered it tight, and tucked it into his coat against the letter. In his book he wrote only one line: **One nine-line spring-return pill, in the bottle. For Dad's knee.**

Send it down he could not. A mixed root a month through the gate, who couldn't even pay the common fund, sending home a pill the Jishi Hall had never seen in its life — Ma San would rap his short club on the doorframe and ask: Shen the Elder, your son up the mountain — whose did he steal? He borrowed a brush at the dispensary and wrote his uncle one line back: Your son is well, don't worry. Tell Dad not to go into the Heisong Ridge. Then he took out three coppers — all he had on him — and pushed them at the barefoot boy. The boy held the coppers and looked at him a long time. "Your uncle said he's paid me the three coppers already." He pushed them back, shouldered his load, and left.

That night at midnight, unable to climb the wall, he crawled out through the drain gap as before, crawled to the herb garden, and pressed a handprint into the box for the thirteenth night in the watch book.

For the half-month after that, Shen Xiaoman kept the night watch with a broken rib.

By day he went to lectures as usual and carried water as usual — one load, three rests, never daring to change shoulders. In the refectory Ma Xiaobao passed his table every day with an empty bowl, stopped every day, and poked that one spot: "Brother, any better?" At each poke his sight went white, and his mouth said, "Better, senior brother."

By night he sat in the east corner of the garden beside Ah He's ring of red thread, among the herbs. His rib hurt and a breath wouldn't go all the way down, so he didn't take it all the way down; he did as the baby in the radish basket did, belly rising, falling, shallow, the fall long. The breath the herbs gave off at night was as thick as the pot his mother cooked at New Year, and breath after breath went down, and the warmth beneath his belly sank a hair each night. Little Zheng squatted at his feet facing the dark, without a sound.

On the night of the fifteenth there was a rustle on top of the wall, and a head came up. Xiaoman didn't move. The figure sat astride the wall, looking all round, and when its look came round to him it stopped.

It was Laonian.

Under the moon the two of them looked at each other across half the garden for a long time — one sitting among the herbs, his face still bruised; one astride the wall, an empty cloth bag in his fist. Laonian's lips moved; nothing came out. Slowly he backed down off the wall; his foot slipped, there was a *thud* outside, then limping footsteps going away.

After dawn Xiaoman found a sheet of oiled paper in the grass at the foot of the wall, folded square, still faintly sweet, with a red stamp on the corner — the stamp of that pastry shop in the county town. In all of Chending Temple only one person could afford that shop's osmanthus cake. He slipped the paper into the watch book. Against that night in the watch book he wrote: **Someone on the wall, went back. Nothing missing. Purple jade ginseng: forty-one.**

The twenty-second of the tenth month, at first light, someone kicked the woodshed door open. Ma Xiaobao stood in the doorway; behind him Zhou Heng, and behind him again his followers — the one with the white cloth round his hand among them. Ma Xiaobao flung aside the heap of straw where Little Zheng slept — and under it, plain as day, lay a purple jade ginseng, its leaves still fresh. "The most valuable thing in the herb garden," said Ma Xiaobao. "A beast is a beast — it can't stop stealing. The watchman keeping the thief — Brother Zhou, how will you write that down?"

Xiaoman crouched, picked the ginseng up, and looked at the cut. The herb gnawed at the west end of the garden on the ninth of the tenth month had a clean stump, but a ragged one — bitten off at one go, tooth marks in rows. This one's stump was smooth: one slanting stroke, flat as a mirror. "Senior Brother," he said, handing the ginseng to Zhou Heng, "a zheng gnaws with its teeth. This one was cut with a knife. There are forty-one purple jade ginseng in the herb garden; I count them every night, and the numbers are all in the watch book. When I came out of the garden at the hour of mao this morning, there were still forty-one. This one isn't the garden's."

Zhou Heng got up and went straight to the herb garden. A stick of incense later he came back, and the ledger had a new line: **Twenty-second of the tenth month. Purple jade ginseng, forty-one, not one missing.** Little Zheng slipped out from by Xiaoman's feet, sniffed twice towards the follower with the cloth round his hand by the door, and went *crack*. The follower put his hand behind his back. Zhou Heng said, "This one doesn't go in the books." He took his ledger and left. Ma Xiaobao bent and picked up the ginseng, squeezed it, and stamped it to pulp.

Six days left to the month's end.

On the night of the twenty-fifth of the tenth month, sitting among the herbs, he let a breath fall, and beneath his belly something went *dong*; the warmth sank suddenly, deeper, like ground dried out all winter when a mattock bites in and turns up another layer; once turned, it could hold twice as much at a stroke. The second level of qi refining.

He had sat it out himself, night after night, with a broken rib.

On the twenty-eighth of the tenth month Zhou Heng did the month-end reckoning; by the time he reached the herb garden's page it was already getting dark. Xiaoman waited at the steward's office door; Ma Xiaobao was there too, with the one whose hand was wrapped in white cloth behind him, and Laonian, standing outside the threshold. Zhou Heng read off the ledger, his finger on it: "The tenth: entered, one spirit beast. From the tenth to today, the herb garden has lost —" he raised his eyes to the one in the doorframe, then lowered them again, "— none."

Xiaoman drew out the oiled paper tucked in the watch book and laid it on the ledger. "On the night of the fifteenth someone came up on the wall, had a look, and went back. At the foot of the wall, this was dropped." A red stamp on the corner. Outside the threshold, Laonian's face went white at once. Xiaoman did not look at him.

Ma Xiaobao took the osmanthus cake out of his mouth. "A bit of oiled paper — who knows where he picked it up?" He stepped in over the threshold and pointed at Xiaoman. "None? Because he ate them himself! Brother Zhou — a skimmer, a month through the gate, sitting night after night in the herb beds, the leaves all leaning his way — he stole herbs and ate himself up a level!"

Xiaoman said, "How does Senior Brother know I sit in the herb beds every night?"

The steward's office went quiet. Ma Xiaobao stood open-mouthed, looked at Zhou Heng, looked at the rafters, and only after a long while got his breath back — and his voice came out higher: "…Get someone to test him! Fetch Master Chu — see if he's the first level or the second!"

That was a real knife. A skimmer, the second level in a month — once that got about, Ma Xiaobao wouldn't need to say another word; the whole outer court would do the rest of the thinking for him.

Xiaoman didn't look at Ma Xiaobao. He said to Zhou Heng, "Senior Brother, please send for Master Chu to test me."

Master Chu had been fetched from the lecture hall, his goat's beard jerking, very impatient. He wasted no words; he clamped Xiaoman's wrist. A thread of cool qi bored in at his wrist and probed inward along the meridians. Xiaoman closed his eyes. This was what the child in the radish basket had taught him — rise, fall; don't haul, don't chase. He drew that second-level warmth in, bit by bit, gathered it into a single grain, drew it into the deepest place beneath his belly, and held it down with a breath — like gripping a red-hot coal in his fist and not being allowed to open it. Wherever Master Chu's qi touched as it probed, it was as if a wire brush had scraped him. He set his teeth and breathed through that not-deep, not-shallow opening; a breath caught the rib, the pain whitened his sight, and still he had to hold it down. Something warm under his nose — a line of blood ran down to his lip. Salty.

Master Chu probed a good while, the time it takes to drink a cup of tea, before he let go and snorted. "First level of qi refining, the qi thin and scattered — one touch and his nose bleeds. A skimmer is still a skimmer." He pressed Xiaoman's ribs too, and at the one on the left his hand stopped. Xiaoman made no sound; the sweat dropped from his forehead bead by bead.

"This bone is still broken," said Master Chu. "Half a month now." He turned to Ma Xiaobao. "The herb garden's herbs are the best thing there is for healing. If he'd stolen and eaten even one, this bone would have knit long ago."

Ma Xiaobao had half swallowed a mouthful of osmanthus cake; it caught in his throat, and he doubled over coughing, and coughed up not a single word.

At the door Master Chu stopped again and looked back, one more look at Xiaoman — at the line of blood under his nose, at the hand clutching his ribs — and in the end asked nothing, and left.

Zhou Heng closed the watch book and put it under the ledger. "I go by the accounts, not by faces." He took up his brush and wrote: **Herb garden night watch: Shen Xiaoman. Wages: culls, one basket a month.** From under the table he lifted a bamboo basket; in it were this month's culls — the insect-bitten, the crooked, the ones with half their qi gone — a small half-basket of them.

Xiaoman carried the basket out of the steward's office. Only now did he dare let go of that grain of warmth he had gripped for the time it takes to drink a cup of tea; the moment he let go it turned three somersaults inside him, and he had to hold the wall and coughed up a mouthful of blood. He wiped his mouth. The chilli-oil bottle in his coat pressed, through the cloth, against the bone that had not knit.

He set the basket down, took out his book, turned to below the line "Rabbits, eleven, nine", and wrote, stroke by stroke: **Twelfth of the tenth month. The woodshed. Twenty-three. Ma Xiaobao.**

When he had written it he drew a line beneath it, and left one box empty under the line. That box was kept for the day of paying it back.

That night, by the well platform in the outer court's back yard, Ma Xiaobao crouched alone, washing his chin with well water. He scrubbed it with soap-pod, ground it with the coarse grit on the well's edge till it was red raw, and the three black spots were still there. He took the porcelain bottle of qi-gathering pills from his coat, turned it upside down, and knocked it against his palm. Three came out — the last three left this month — dull grey, one line, a ring of black spots round the line, exactly like the ones on his chin.

He thought of Shen Xiaoman's broken bone, of the oiled paper in Zhou Heng's ledger, of that one foundation pill — the twelfth month, the champion, the only one in the whole sect. He thought: what makes him so special? Then he thought: he takes one mouthful, I take three.

He swallowed the three pills at one go, without even water — dry, his neck stretching and stretching with it. The warmth came up, hot, burning his face red, setting the three black spots on his chin throbbing. He set his teeth and dug his nails into the cracks of the well stones, waiting for it to pass. He stood up, wiped his mouth, took another osmanthus cake from his sleeve, and bit into it. Still hungry.

Early the next morning a new notice went up on the outer court's notice board, the ink not yet dry:

**The Chending hidden realm opens once in ten years. The first of the eleventh month — all outer-court disciples may enter.**
